o: Both branches of every posterior ramus supply muscle
But only one, medial or lateral, reaches skin. (Last's p. 19)
The posterior rami of C7 and C8 reach the skin
The lower two cervical and lower two lumbar posterior rami fail to reach the skin, as does C1. (Last's p. 19)
Medial branches give the cutaneous supply in the upper half of the body
Lateral branches in the lower half; the change is at about T6. (Last's p. 19-20)
Posterior rami supply some limb muscles in man
Last's: no posterior ramus ever supplies limb skin or muscle in any vertebrate. (Last's p. 19)
Where nerve and segmental artery cross, the nerve lies nearer the skin
So the nerve circle surrounds the arterial circle. (Last's p. 20)
The collateral branches of intercostal nerves carry cutaneous fibres
They contain motor fibres only. (Last's p. 20)
The sympathetic trunk lies anterior to the segmental vessels from skull to coccyx
Which lie anterior to the spinal nerves. (Last's p. 20)
In the neurovascular plane the nerves lie above the arteries
They lie below them. (Last's p. 20)
Limb buds grow out from the strip supplied by lateral branches of anterior rami
(Last's p. 21)
The anterior divisions of limb plexuses supply the extensor compartments
They supply flexors; posterior divisions supply extensors. (Last's p. 21)
No S3 fibres enter the extensor compartment of the lower limb
Like T1 in the upper limb, the lowest root goes entirely to flexors. (Last's p. 22)
The short head of biceps femoris is supplied by the tibial part of the sciatic
It is supplied by the peroneal part; it developed in the extensor compartment. (Last's p. 22)
There is no dermatome overlap across axial lines
So always test across axial lines. (Last's p. 23)
The upper limb posterior axial line reaches the wrist
It reaches only the deltoid insertion; the anterior line almost reaches the wrist. (Last's p. 23)
The central root of the limb plexus clothes the peripheral extremity
C7 in the upper limb. (Last's p. 23)
Lower limb skin is borrowed symmetrically from cranial and caudal sides
All four borrowed dermatomes (T12–L3) are cranial. (Last's p. 24)
Anaesthetizing the anterior third of the scrotum needs L1
The posterior two-thirds is S3, seven segments lower. (Last's p. 24)
Last's considers posterior axial lines well established
Probably they do not exist; anterior axial line evidence is better. (Last's p. 24)
S4 supplies the immediate perianal skin
S3 is the sitting area. (Last's p. 24)
The great toe is usually supplied by L4
Usually by L5, though L4 may extend along its medial side. (Last's p. 25)
T1 supplies the medial elbow but not the axilla
T2 supplies the axilla. (Last's p. 25)
Last's places the nipple firmly at T5
T4, or T5 according to some. (Last's p. 25)
L3 supplies the anterior and medial knee
(Last's p. 25)
L4 supplies the lateral malleolus
L4 is the medial malleolus; S1 the lateral. (Last's p. 25)
For each joint one segment more distal, the spinal centre lies one segment lower
(Last's p. 25)
Wrist flexion and extension are supplied by different segments
Both are C6, 7; digit flexion and extension both C7, 8. (Last's p. 27)
Tibialis posterior is supplied by L4 unlike neighbouring plantar flexors
Matching its inverting partner tibialis anterior. (Last's p. 26)
Gluteus maximus is L4, 5, S1
Obturator internus and gluteus maximus are L5, S1, 2; other buttock muscles L4, 5, S1. (Last's p. 26-7)
Last's lists S2 for the small muscles of the foot
(Last's p. 28)
In nerve root lesions proper, sweating in the territory is reduced
It is normal; grey rami join distal to the roots. (Last's p. 28)
Tendon reflexes are the only monosynaptic reflex arcs
(Last's p. 28)
Last's gives the knee jerk as L4
As L3. (Last's p. 28)
An extensor plantar response is normal under 1 year
Until corticospinal myelination in the second year. (Last's p. 29)
In Beevor's sign the umbilicus moves downwards
It moves upwards from weakness below the umbilicus. (Last's p. 29)
The anal and bulbocavernosus reflexes depend mainly on S3
(Last's p. 29-30)
Hyperreflexia in UMN lesions is driven through Ia afferents from cortex
γ motor neurons are driven by reticulospinal and vestibulospinal fibres. (Last's p. 28)
In only about 10% are T1 cells involved in upper limb sympathetic supply
T1 mostly serves head and neck; the lowest level may be T10. (Last's p. 30)
The white ramus is the more proximal of the two rami
The white ramus is the more distal. (Last's p. 30)
There are usually 11 thoracic, 4 lumbar and 4 sacral sympathetic ganglia
One fewer than the nerves. (Last's p. 30)
Grey rami contain afferent fibres
Grey rami contain only postganglionic efferents; white rami carry preganglionic and afferent fibres. (Last's p. 32)
Sacral splanchnic nerves are sympathetic
Pelvic splanchnic nerves are parasympathetic. (Last's p. 31)
Visceral afferent cell bodies lie in the sympathetic ganglia
They lie in posterior root ganglia. (Last's p. 32)
Intraneural ganglia may explain anomalous sympathectomy results
(Last's p. 32)
Limb vessels receive sympathetic fibres that run long distances along the arteries
Fibres run with peripheral nerves and leave near the target. (Last's p. 32)
Upper limb sympathectomy removes the second and third thoracic ganglia
T1 is preserved to avoid Horner's. (Last's p. 32-3)
Lumbar sympathectomy removes the first and second lumbar ganglia
It removes L3 and L4; L1 is preserved for ejaculation. (Last's p. 33)
Lumbar ganglia have no constant relation to the vertebrae
(Last's p. 33)
The gonads receive a parasympathetic supply
Suprarenals and gonads appear to have only sympathetic supply. (Last's p. 33)
Only the parasympathetic root relays in a cranial parasympathetic ganglion
(Last's p. 33)
The ciliary ganglion parasympathetic root comes via the nerve to superior rectus
It comes via the nerve to inferior oblique (inferior division). (Last's p. 33)
The sympathetic root of the submandibular ganglion comes with the facial artery
(Last's p. 34)
The sensory root of the ciliary ganglion comes from the frontal nerve
It comes from the nasociliary nerve. (Last's p. 34)
The otic ganglion has an additional somatic motor root
From the nerve to medial pterygoid, to the two tensors. (Last's p. 35)
The sympathetic root of the otic ganglion runs with the internal carotid
It runs with the middle meningeal artery. (Last's p. 35)
Pelvic splanchnic afferent cell bodies lie in S2–4 dorsal root ganglia
(Last's p. 35)
Vagal visceral afferent cell bodies lie in the superior vagal ganglion
They lie in the inferior ganglia of IX and X. (Last's p. 35)
Implantation occurs about 6 days after fertilization
(Last's p. 35)
Sclerotomes give rise to the muscles of the body wall
Sclerotomes give vertebrae and dura; myotomes give body wall muscle. (Last's p. 36)
The suprarenal cortex arises from the intermediate cell mass
Its medial side also gives the gonad. (Last's p. 36)
Limb muscles develop from migrating paraxial myotomes
They develop in situ from lateral plate mesoderm. (Last's p. 36)
The diaphragm muscle comes mainly from the fourth cervical myotome
(Last's p. 37)
The buccopharyngeal membrane persists until the eighth week
It disappears in the third week. (Last's p. 37)
There are four pharyngeal pouches separating six arches
The fourth and fifth open by a common groove. (Last's p. 37)
Arch arteries are more constant during development than arch nerves
Nerves remain constant; vascular patterns change. (Last's p. 37)
The lingula is a persistent part of Meckel's cartilage
As are occasional ossa mentalia. (Last's p. 38)
The maxillary process is derived from Meckel's cartilage
It is not. (Last's p. 38)
The mandible ossifies in membrane at the sixth week
(Last's p. 38)
The anterior ligament of the malleus is a second arch derivative
It is first arch. (Last's p. 38)
Levator palati is a fourth/sixth arch derivative
Supplied by vagal branches. (Last's p. 39)
The first pouch has widely separated ectoderm and endoderm
It is the only pouch where they stay closely apposed, at the drum. (Last's p. 39)
Thymic cortical lymphocytes migrated from bone marrow
The medulla and Hassall's corpuscles come from the thymic bud. (Last's p. 39)
Thyroglossal cysts commonly lie in front of the hyoid body
Commonly behind it, as the duct is kinked by the bone. (Last's p. 39)
The third arch artery forms part of the internal carotid
(Last's p. 40)
The right fourth arch artery forms the brachiocephalic trunk
It forms the right subclavian; the left fourth forms the aortic arch. (Last's p. 40)
The fifth arch artery disappears entirely
(Last's p. 40)
The dorsal part of the right sixth arch artery persists
It disappears on the right; on the left it is the ductus arteriosus. (Last's p. 40)
A retro-oesophageal right subclavian occurs when the right fourth arch disappears
And the distal right dorsal aorta persists; the right recurrent nerve is then non-recurrent. (Last's p. 41)
A right aortic arch occurs when the right fourth arch disappears
It occurs when the left fourth arch and dorsal aorta disappear. (Last's p. 41)
Sternocleidomastoid always lies behind a branchial fistula
It migrates from a dorsal source. (Last's p. 41)
A branchial fistula usually passes lateral to the external carotid
It passes between the external and internal carotids. (Last's p. 41)
In man the whole upper lip including the philtrum comes from the maxillary processes
(Last's p. 42)
The frontonasal process forms the philtrum
It normally forms no part of the upper lip. (Last's p. 42)
Harelip occurs in about 1 in 1000 births
Cleft palate about 1 in 2500. (Last's p. 43)
Complete cleft palate usually runs between canine and first premolar
It usually runs between lateral incisor and canine. (Last's p. 43)
The palatal processes and septum unite from before backwards
So a bifid uvula is the mildest defect. (Last's p. 43)
A facial cleft along the nasolacrimal line results from failure of the median and lateral nasal processes
It results from failure of the lateral nasal and maxillary processes. (Last's p. 43)
The ureter opens into the urogenital sinus at a higher level than the mesonephric duct
(Last's p. 43-4)
The genital tubercle forms the labia minora
It forms the clitoris; the urogenital folds form the labia minora. (Last's p. 44)
The site of the buccopharyngeal membrane cannot be identified with certainty in the adult
It breaks down in the third week. (Last's p. 37)
Hassall's corpuscles come from bone-marrow-derived cells
They come from the thymic bud; cortical lymphocytes come from marrow. (Last's p. 39)
The dorsal diverticulum of the second pouch forms the inferior parathyroid
It helps form the tympanic cavity; the third pouch gives the inferior parathyroid. (Last's p. 39)
The left fourth arch artery forms the left subclavian
It forms the arch of the aorta. (Last's p. 40)
Parasympathetic fibres supply the arrectores pilorum
Parasympathetic supply is wholly visceral. (Last's p. 33)
The superior cervical ganglion gives four grey rami
The other cervical ganglia two each. (Last's p. 31)
Sympathetic cardiac branches arise only from thoracic ganglia
Cervical ganglia give cardiac branches too. (Last's p. 31)
Visceral afferents reach the spinal nerve through the white ramus
(Last's p. 32)
C4 skin over the deltoid is borrowed from the neck
T2 is borrowed for the axilla. (Last's p. 24)
The lower limb anterior axial line spirals to the back of the calf almost to the heel
(Last's p. 24)
L5 and S1 have been reported to reach buttock skin, though this is not usually expected
(Last's p. 24)
L4 lies over the fibula
L4 is over the tibia; L5 over the fibula. (Last's p. 24)
